findings.title: Four spectrumColor HSL copies → one harmonicColor backed by sampleColorRamp OKLCH ramp
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/lib/canvas-drawing/transforms.ts:3 (`spectrumColor` — `(1-curved)*300` HSL hue), web/src/components/equation/FrequencyGraph.vue:42 (identical copy), web/src/components/equation/lib/harmonics.ts:81 (copy with alpha param), web/src/components/visualization/lib/canvas-drawing/epicycles.ts:162 (imports from transforms). All four use sRGB-HSL which is non-perceptual (equal hue steps do not produce equal perceived colour distances) and drift away from the favicon's brand palette. The live-workspace.jpeg and live-equation.jpeg show the epicycle circles and convergence legend using the magentar→red HSL sweep — visually plausible but not the brand colours.
findings.current_state: Four independent `spectrumColor` functions hand-roll `hsl(${hue}, 85%, 55%)` with a `(1-t)*300` hue mapping. This is sRGB-HSL, not perceptual; it has no gamut mapping; it bears no relation to the favicon's R-O-Y-G-B-V stops (#ff4444 → #8844ff); it is duplicated 4× with no shared contract. The ConvergenceLegend and CoefficientsSpectrum also import these copies (ConvergenceLegend.vue:3, CoefficientsSpectrum.vue:47). M-design-language.md §3.1 cites all four as 'C7-3' but the proposed replacement still uses `mixColorsN` for the interim.
findings.proposed: M.W7 authors ONE `lib/colors.ts` export `harmonicColor(i: number, total: number, alpha = 1): string` that samples position `i/(total-1)` from a module-level `HARMONIC_RAMP: Color[]` (6 gamut-mapped OKLCH stops) built once from the favicon's start/end stops via `sampleColorRamp`. The ramp is constructed: `sampleColorRamp(color2(parseHex('#ff4444'), 'oklch'), color2(parseHex('#8844ff'), 'oklch'), 6, { space: 'oklch', hueMethod: 'longer', gamutMap: true })`. `harmonicColor` linearly indexes the pre-built array, calls `color2(stop, 'rgb').toString()` for a CSS-safe `rgb(…)` string. All four `spectrumColor` call-sites are replaced with one import. The `STATIC.rainbow` twin in `colors.ts:12–18` is deleted — the computed `HARMONIC_RAMP` is the only palette. The 118-line bespoke parser (`cssVarToHex`, `hslToHex`, `rgbToHex`) is replaced by `color2()` + `Color.toString()` for the two remaining callers (`resolveVizColors`).

findings.title: safeAccentColor not used — per-route accent contrast is ad-hoc D.W4 amber override, not systematic
findings.evidence: web/src/lib/colors.ts has no import of `safeAccentColor` or `needsContrastAdjustment` from value.js. M-design-language.md §3.2 references `safeAccentColor` and `needsContrastAdjustment` as load-bearing, but the adoption gap survives into the bump. The `--viz-amber` local `:root` override in web/style.css:113–126 (a D.W4 axe-AA patch, carried D→I per M.md §10) is the current contrast guard — a static hardcoded lightness shift for exactly one colour, not a systematic floor. user-critique/08-dropdown-glass-darkened.png and user-critique/09-buttons-invisible-unhovered.png both show the amber/tonal accent applied inconsistently: the active Equation route item in the dropdown is amber (ramp[3] green was the intent from M-design-language.md §3.2), and the preset pills have no idle tonal fill.
findings.current_state: `safeAccentColor(color, bgLightness)` and `needsContrastAdjustment` are exported by value.js 0.13 (index.ts:152–155) but never imported in fourier. The per-route `--route-accent` system described in M-design-language.md §3.2 has no implementation; the nav active state maps all routes to `--viz-amber` (AppHeader.vue:197–198). The `--viz-amber` light-mode override is a known chronic that M.md §10 books with a kill-date ('deletes on adopt'). The tonal-accent recipe (`accent-tone`) is a glass-ui ask that glass-ui BB's `W-CROSSREPO-ASKS` may or may not ship; without it fourier must derive the 3-channel `--accent-fill/--accent-edge/--accent-ink` from the same `safeAccentColor` logic.
findings.proposed: M.W7 sources every accent from the `HARMONIC_RAMP` via a `routeAccent(routeName: RouteName): OKLCHColor` helper that: (1) picks the ramp stop for the route (paper=0, visualize=1, gallery=2, equation=3, morph=4); (2) passes it through `safeAccentColor(stop, bgLightness, 0.35)` where `bgLightness` is resolved once from the glass-ui ladder rung of the current route's primary surface (BAND 1 `glass-resting` ≈ 0.65 in dark, ≈ 0.35 in light — read once from a `getOklchLightness(color2(parseCSSVar('--background'), 'oklch'))` call at mount). The emitted `oklch(L C H)` string is written to `--route-accent` on `:root` at mount + on theme toggle. The `--viz-amber` `:root` override in `style.css:113–126` is deleted at M.W7 close (the systematic `safeAccentColor` floor makes it redundant — the kill-date is now M.W7, not a forward book). The glass-ui `accent-tone` ask remains in `ADOPTION-ASKS.md §11` as the upstream improvement (BB's `W-CROSSREPO-ASKS`); the fourier-local derivation from `safeAccentColor` is the no-wait floor.

findings.title: Harmonic colour sweeps on the canvas are sRGB drift — should be OKLCH-animated with sampleColorRamp
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/lib/canvas-drawing/epicycles.ts:162 calls `spectrumColor(i, nVis)` per frame per epicycle arm. The colour is recomputed from the HSL formula every animation frame — no memoisation, no gamut management. The convergence-reveal signature (M.W9) will call `harmonicColor` per harmonic per frame as partials accumulate; with the current sRGB-HSL path this produces a non-perceptual hue sweep. M-motion-architecture.md (not yet read) describes the convergence-reveal as THE signature; it must use the perceptual ramp. live-workspace.jpeg shows the canvas in an empty/unloaded state so the in-motion behaviour is inferred from the source.
findings.current_state: Every canvas drawing call that needs a harmonic colour recomputes `spectrumColor(i, total)` inline, producing a fresh `hsl(…)` string from an HSL hue formula. There is no concept of a pre-baked ramp; the colour model is sRGB-HSL with no gamut management. For the convergence-reveal (M.W9), each partial sum would accumulate with a hue step that is perceptually non-uniform — the visual impression of 'convergence' is tied to how evenly the hues feel distinct, which sRGB-HSL cannot guarantee.
findings.proposed: The module-level `HARMONIC_RAMP: Color[]` from E4-02 is the canonical source for all canvas colour. `harmonicColor(i, total)` for canvas use SHOULD pre-convert each stop to `rgb` (stored as `RGBColor`) and cache the float channels (r, g, b ∈ [0,1]) in a parallel `HARMONIC_RAMP_RGB: [number, number, number][]` array. Canvas `ctx.strokeStyle = `rgba(${r*255|0}, ${g*255|0}, ${b*255|0}, ${alpha})`` avoids string allocation on the hot path. For the convergence-reveal animation (M.W9), the partial-sum harmonic accumulation staggers through the ramp in OKLCH order — the perceptual evenness of the `oklch hueMethod:'longer'` arc ensures each new harmonic feels visually distinct, not washed-out or clustered. `sampleColorRamp` with `endpoints:'exclusive'` is used when `total` is unknown at ramp-build time: build a fixed 64-stop ramp, index by `Math.round(i / (total-1) * 63)`.

findings.title: Morph-stroke and palette-transition colour paths are sRGB — should be OKLCH perceptual arcs
findings.evidence: M-design-language.md §3.3 states 'the morph stroke (colour encodes morph state, C7-5)'; live-morph.jpeg shows the morph stage. The current morph stroke hue is a CSS transition or manual lerp in HSL/hex — not using value.js perceptual interpolation. The gallery tier tokens (`--tier-featured`, `--tier-saved`) are resolved via `cssVarToHex` (the 118-line parser) + sRGB-HSL; they do not go through `mixColors`/`sampleColorRamp`. M-design-language.md §3.2 says 'Notation/tier/energy hues source from value.js: the trig/exp/polar pill tints + the energy/tier ramp become value.js triads/interpolated scales (B4-04, B4-05)'.
findings.current_state: Palette transitions (the morph stroke sweeping through morph states, convergence legend updating as harmonics add) use CSS `transition: color` (sRGB interpolation) or inline HSL recomputation. The colour distance between morph states is visually non-uniform because sRGB interpolation crosses the neutral grey axis. The gallery tier and equation notation pill tints are hardcoded Tailwind hex / raw HSL with no relation to the brand ramp.
findings.proposed: M.W7 authors `paletteLerp(from: OKLCHColor, to: OKLCHColor, t: number): string` — a thin wrapper over `mixColors(color2(from,'oklch'), color2(to,'oklch'), 1-t, t, 'oklch', 'shorter').toString()` — used for the morph stroke colour interpolation (morph state maps to a position on the ramp; `paletteLerp` drives the stroke as the morph t advances). For the gallery tier badges and equation notation pills, `sampleColorRamp` samples a 3-stop triad (trig=ramp[0], exp=ramp[2], polar=ramp[4]) with `gamutMap:true`; the emitted oklch strings are written to `--pill-trig`, `--pill-exp`, `--pill-polar` CSS vars at mount. No hard-coded Tailwind hex survives at any tinted pill site. The 118-line `cssVarToHex` parser is deleted; `resolveVizColors` is rewritten using `color2(parseCSSOklch(getComputedStyle(…).getPropertyValue(varName)), 'rgb').toString()` — a two-line replacement using value.js idiomatically.

glassui_asks.name: glass-ui-accent-tone
glassui_asks.what: A contrast-floored 3-channel tonal accent composable (`--accent-fill` / `--accent-edge` / `--accent-ink`) from a single `--tone` prop — the systematic per-route tonal-accent system. fourier re-derives this recipe ~57 times (pills, toggles, badges, swatches) using inline `color-mix(in oklch, …)`. BB's `W-CROSSREPO-ASKS` is the intake channel.
glassui_asks.why: E4-03 establishes that fourier's current floor is a static `--viz-amber` D.W4 override and the `safeAccentColor` systematic replacement. When `accent-tone` ships in glass-ui 4.1.0, the fourier-local `safeAccentColor` derivation deletes and every tonal accent inherits the platform primitive. Without it, fourier must carry the derivation as an acknowledged interim (acceptable — the floor exists, is correct, and is not a workaround).

open_questions: sampleColorRamp(from, to, n) produces a 2-endpoint ramp; the favicon has 6 distinct stops (#ff4444 #ff8800 #ffcc00 #44bb44 #4488ff #8844ff). The correct approach for a 6-stop brand ramp is either (a) call sampleColorRamp once per adjacent pair and concatenate (5 segments × k stops each) or (b) use mixColorsN with the 6 stops as explicit anchors. Which idiom M.W7 chooses affects the ramp's perceptual uniformity — the adjacent-pair approach honours the brand hues exactly while allowing smooth interpolation between them, whereas mixColorsN folds to a centroid. This is a design decision for M.W7 execution.

The canvas hot-path caches HARMONIC_RAMP_RGB as float triples to avoid per-frame string allocation. When total (number of harmonics) varies at runtime, the ramp must either be rebuilt or indexed with a normalised position. A fixed 64-stop ramp indexed by round(i/(total-1)*63) is proposed — but if total > 64, the last few harmonics alias to the same stop. Confirm the maximum harmonic count to set the ramp depth.

The `--viz-amber` override kill-date (M.md §10) was previously 'value.js safeAccentColor makes it systematic; local override deletes on adopt'. E4-03 proposes that adopt = M.W7. Confirm this accelerated kill-date is acceptable — the override deletes at M.W7 close, not at a glass-ui BB adoption event.

value.js 0.13 ships `sampleColorRamp` with `gamutMap: true` by default (mix.ts:104). For the canvas HARMONIC_RAMP the gamut-mapped stops are RGB-safe. For CSS custom property emission (`--icon-ramp-0..5`), the stops should be emitted as `oklch(L C H)` (valid in Tailwind v4 / modern browsers). Confirm that the target browser floor for this project accepts `oklch()` in CSS custom property values — if not, emit `color(display-p3 …)` or `rgb(…)` as the fallback.

The morph-stroke `paletteLerp` proposed in E4-05 calls `mixColors` at animation-frame rate. At 60 fps this is one `color2` conversion + one `mixColors` call per frame — acceptable for a single stroke but not for a per-harmonic loop. If the morph route ever animates N harmonics simultaneously with individual hue transitions, the ramp-index approach (E4-04) should be used instead of per-frame `paletteLerp`. Confirm the morph stroke is a single-stroke global colour (not per-harmonic) before choosing the approach.

E5.verdict: Eight hand-rolled rAF loops remain across the codebase (animation.ts, ConvergencePlot, useCanvasHover ×2, PaperView progress, useScrollNavigation ×4+ measure loops). Two are verbatim ping-pong duplicates. The keyframes.js 4.3.0 light tier — the canonical replacement — is installed but consumed only in useFourierMorph, which itself uses the `Animation` engine path rather than the lighter `SmoothProgress`/`NumericAnimation` composables. Three CSS infinite-loop animations lack PRM guards (rainbow-slide, golden-shimmer-css, rainbow-drift is guarded). The `--ease-apple-spring` token used at six fourier sites is absent from glass-ui 4.0's token sheet; it resolves to `unset`, degrading those transitions to browser-default `ease`. The tab-panel slide animation uses a bare `ease-out` keyword rather than a design token. The ConvergencePlot rAF loop auto-starts on mount with no PRM gate and no IntersectionObserver off-screen parking — it burns CPU on a hidden tab. The GlassTimeline caret uses an `ease` keyword. The M.W9 motion-architecture wave correctly identifies all of these as the target; the audit hardens its scope and adds three missing site-level sub-findings the prior plan does not name explicitly.

findings.title: Duplicate ping-pong rAF clock in ConvergencePlot (verbatim copy of animation.ts)
findings.evidence: web/src/components/equation/ConvergencePlot.vue:57–70 mirrors animation.ts:51–75 exactly — same elapsed/cycle/frac/ping-pong arithmetic, same rafId pattern, local `playing` ref, local `loopStartTime`.
findings.current_state: ConvergencePlot owns its own autonomous rAF clock with no shared playhead, no IntersectionObserver off-screen gating, and no PRM guard on the `startLoop()` call at `onMounted` line 324. It auto-plays without checking `prefers-reduced-motion`.
findings.proposed: M.W9: extract `useFourierPlayhead` (the unified clock already specified in design/M-motion-architecture.md). ConvergencePlot subscribes to the shared `t`/`easedT` reactive state; the rAF loop and the local `playing` ref are deleted. Off-screen parking rides the shared IntersectionObserver reference count already wired in animation.ts. PRM: the shared playhead checks `window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` at `play()` and parks at `t=0` (terminal state) rather than playing.

findings.title: ConvergencePlot rAF loop: no PRM gate on auto-play at mount
findings.evidence: web/src/components/equation/ConvergencePlot.vue:323–324: `onMounted(() => { nextTick(() => { draw(); t.value = 0; playing.value = true; startLoop(); }); ...`. No `prefers-reduced-motion` check precedes `startLoop()`. The equation tab is visible on page load and the loop fires unconditionally for every user.
findings.current_state: Auto-plays the convergence animation without honouring the user's reduced-motion preference. WCAG 2.3.3 violation; inv-34 breach.
findings.proposed: M.W9: gate `startLoop()` behind a PRM check — if `window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches`, call `draw()` once at a static representative `t` (e.g. `t=1`) and remain paused. The unified `useFourierPlayhead` handles this centrally so no per-component guard is needed at the call site.

findings.title: ConvergencePlot rAF loop: no IntersectionObserver off-screen parking
findings.evidence: web/src/components/equation/ConvergencePlot.vue:57–70, onMounted:323–326. Loop runs continuously while `playing.value` is true regardless of tab visibility or scroll position. Contrast animation.ts:43–106 which reference-counts `visibleCanvases` via IntersectionObserver and parks the clock when no canvas is on-screen.
findings.current_state: The Equation tab's convergence canvas burns a 60fps rAF clock when the user is on the Paper tab, the Gallery, or has scrolled past the canvas. On a mobile device this is a continuous battery drain. The `BasisCanvas` already implements the correct I.γ pattern.
findings.proposed: M.W9: the `useFourierPlayhead` composable inherits the `setCanvasVisible(bool)` reference-count contract from the unified animation store. ConvergencePlot mounts an IntersectionObserver on `containerRef` and calls `setCanvasVisible` on intersection changes — identical to BasisCanvas:435–452. No bespoke logic needed once the shared playhead is adopted.

findings.title: useCanvasHover: two additional rAF loops (scale lerp + shimmer) outside the shared clock
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/composables/useCanvasHover.ts:52–82. `hoverAnimFrame` drives an exponential-decay scale lerp (`currentScale += diff * 0.12`) at uncapped frame rate. `shimmerRafId` drives a separate shimmer tick that calls `onRedraw()` every frame while any basis is hovered. Both are independent rAF loops not coordinated with `animation.ts`.
findings.current_state: Two rAF loops fire in parallel with the main epicycle clock — potentially three simultaneous rAF callbacks on the same canvas when playing + hovering. The shimmer tick fires `onRedraw` independently of the animation clock's `drawFrame` watcher, causing redundant full-canvas clears per 16ms frame. The scale lerp is a hand-rolled spring that predates keyframes.js 4.3's `SpringProgress`.
findings.proposed: M.W9: transpose `updateHoverScale` to `SpringProgress` from `@mkbabb/keyframes.js` (the light-tier composable the M plan names explicitly). `SpringProgress` emits a reactive scalar; `BasisCanvas`'s render watcher already fires on `anim.t` changes — add `hoverScale` to the watcher deps and eliminate the separate rAF. The shimmer is a `performance.now()` sinusoid (golden-shimmer.ts:12) sampled per draw — it requires no independent loop; removing the shimmer rAF and sampling in the main draw pass is sufficient (the value is already computed inline in `goldenShimmerAlpha()`).

findings.title: PaperView scroll-progress: rAF loop fallback never disabled on Page Visibility change
findings.evidence: web/src/components/paper/PaperView.vue:157–186. `armProgressFallback()` attaches a passive `scroll` listener that schedules a rAF to write `scaleX` to `.paper-progress-bar`. The loop parks correctly between scroll events (one-shot rAF, not a continuous loop), but there is no `visibilitychange` listener to flush `progressRaf` when the tab goes hidden. If the user switches tabs mid-scroll the outstanding rAF fires in the hidden state.
findings.current_state: Minor: one orphaned rAF fires on tab-hide. The native `animation-timeline: scroll()` path (`NATIVE_SCROLL_TIMELINE`) skips this fallback and is already preferred. The fallback is the JS floor for browsers without scroll-driven animations.
findings.proposed: Add `document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.hidden) disarmProgressFallback(); else armProgressFallback(); })` in the `onMounted` block and remove the listener in `onUnmounted`. This is a one-line add, consistent with the existing `disarmProgressFallback` pattern. No library needed.

findings.title: useScrollNavigation: multiple layout-sync rAF calls outside the unified clock
findings.evidence: web/src/components/paper/useScrollNavigation.ts:89, 106, 138, 159, 163, 187. Six `requestAnimationFrame` call-sites drive a correction loop (`correct()`) and overlay fade logic. These are layout-measurement rAFs, not animation rAFs.
findings.current_state: Correctly categorised as layout-sync measure loops (the M plan's documented exemption: 'layout-sync measure loops exempt + doc-marked', M.md:64/117). However they are undocumented at the call sites — the inv-34 requirement is that exempt loops are 'doc-marked'.
findings.proposed: Add a brief inline comment above each `requestAnimationFrame` call in useScrollNavigation.ts marking it as a layout-sync measure loop (e.g. `// layout-sync: waiting for Vue DOM patch / section mount before measuring scroll target`). This is not a refactor — it is the doc-marking the invariant requires so future audits do not misclassify them.

findings.title: useFourierMorph: keyframes.js Animation engine used; should be NumericAnimation/Sequence light tier
findings.evidence: web/src/composables/useFourierMorph.ts:14, 38–43, 127–143. Imports `loadAnimationEngine` + constructs an `Animation` with `addFrame`/`parse`/`play` — the full engine path. The morph uses it purely as a tween duration controller: it adds a dummy `v: '0px' → v: '1px'` frame and only reads `time / a.options.duration` in the tick callback.
findings.current_state: The `Animation` engine (which carries value.js) is lazily loaded, which is correct bundle-wise. But the usage pattern is a tween clock — a single scalar from 0→1 over a duration — which is the exact primitive keyframes.js 4.3's `NumericAnimation` (light tier, no value.js) provides. The three-phase sequence (settle-out → morph → settle-in) maps to `Sequence`.
findings.proposed: M.W9: transpose `useFourierMorph` to `NumericAnimation` + `Sequence` from the keyframes.js 4.3 light tier. Each phase becomes a `NumericAnimation({ from: 0, to: 1, duration, easing })` composable; the `Sequence` chains them. The lazy `loadAnimationEngine` boundary is deleted. The easing functions are passed as the `easing` option (keyframes.js 4.3 accepts `resolveEasing` strings or functions). The morph `tick` callbacks become `onUpdate` handlers.

findings.title: `--ease-apple-spring` token absent from glass-ui 4.0 — six fourier sites resolve to unset/initial
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/gallery/GalleryCard.vue:196; GallerySearchBar.vue:188–189; VisualizationView.vue:426; AppHeader.vue:280; GalleryCard.vue:295. `grep -r 'ease-apple-spring' web/node_modules/@mkbabb/glass-ui/dist/` returns zero CSS hits. The glass-ui 4.0 token sheet (scheme-motion.css) defines `--ease-apple` (the micro-interaction cubic-bezier) and `--spring-{smooth,snappy,bouncy,gentle}` (linear() spring registers) but not `--ease-apple-spring`. The README mentions it only in a legacy table.
findings.current_state: All six `var(--ease-apple-spring)` references resolve to `unset`, which CSS falls back to the browser-default `ease` keyword. The intended springy-overshoot hover/card transition reads as a flat deceleration. This is a silent regression introduced by the M.W1 glass-ui 4.0 bump.
findings.proposed: M.W9 (or M.W1 migration sweep): replace `var(--ease-apple-spring)` with the semantically correct glass-ui 4.0 spring token at each site: card lift/hover → `var(--spring-smooth)` + `var(--spring-smooth-duration)` (the one-button/hover register per scheme-motion.css:163–174); like-bounce → `var(--spring-bouncy)` + `var(--spring-bouncy-duration)` (emphatic micro); expand-pop enter → `var(--spring-bouncy)`; GallerySearchBar filter drawer → `var(--spring-snappy)`. Each `transition` must pair the spring with its companion `-duration` token so the settle is physically timed, not an arbitrary 0.25s.
findings.wave_hint: M.W1 migration sweep (or M.W9 easing unification)

findings.title: Tab-panel slide-in uses bare `ease-out` keyword, not a design token
findings.evidence: web/src/style.css:84: `animation: tab-slide-in 0.18s ease-out;`. The `@keyframes tab-slide-in` at lines 87–89 uses the CSS keyword `ease-out`, not `var(--ease-out)` or `var(--ease-standard)`. This is the sole global-scope animation in style.css.
findings.current_state: Inconsistent with the A.W3.d discipline (bezier→token) applied everywhere else. `ease-out` is the CSS keyword cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1) — numerically identical to `--ease-out` but not token-unified, meaning a future token change would leave this site behind. Also noted: the comment at style.css:10–11 says this is 'filed upstream as glass-ui carries' — it should be tracked as a glass-ui ask if glass-ui's SegmentedTabs does not already ship this animation natively in 4.0.
findings.proposed: Change `ease-out` to `var(--ease-standard)` (the canonical enter easing per scheme-motion.css usage). Book to glass-ui BB `W-CROSSREPO-ASKS` the ask that `<SegmentedTabs>` ships its own tab-panel entry animation so fourier's global selector can be deleted once glass-ui owns it.

findings.title: rainbow-slide (ImageUpload) and golden-shimmer CSS (ContourEditorCanvas) have no PRM guard
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/ImageUpload.vue:159: `animation: rainbow-slide 1.4s linear infinite` — no `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block in that file. web/src/components/visualization/ContourEditorCanvas.vue:324: `animation: golden-shimmer 1.2s ease-in-out infinite` — no PRM block in that file either.
findings.current_state: Two CSS infinite-loop animations (the image-upload drag-border rainbow and the contour-canvas point shimmer) run unconditionally, violating WCAG 2.3.3 and inv-34 (the motion-proportion floor). Contrast GalleryMarquee.vue:126–132 and AnimationControls.vue:178–179 which correctly guard their infinite CSS animations behind `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { animation: none; }`.
findings.proposed: Add `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .drag-border { animation: none; } }` to ImageUpload.vue and `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .selected-point { animation: none; } }` to ContourEditorCanvas.vue. These are two-line adds; no architectural change needed. M.W9 closes the 'three PRM gaps' cited in the plan — this finding names two of the three explicitly.

findings.title: GlassTimeline caret uses bare `ease` keyword and raw box-shadow tokens
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/GlassTimeline.vue:96: `transition: opacity 0.2s ease;` and line 116: `box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);` (raw RGBA, not a `--shadow-*` token).
findings.current_state: Two micro-violations of the A.W3.d token discipline. The caret is a tooltip-like popover; the canonical glass-ui pattern for such elements uses `--shadow-popover` and `var(--ease-standard)`.
findings.proposed: Change `ease` → `var(--ease-standard)`. Replace `box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` with `box-shadow: var(--shadow-popover)` (or the nearest shadow token in glass-ui 4.0's scale). Token unification; no behaviour change.

findings.title: GalleryMarquee will-change: transform without containment — compositor layer leak
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/gallery/GalleryMarquee.vue:95: `.marquee-inner { will-change: transform; }`. The element is `width: max-content` (unbounded inline width) with no explicit `contain` property. On gallery views with many cards this promotes a very large composited layer.
findings.current_state: `will-change: transform` on an unbounded `max-content` element creates a compositor layer whose rasterisation size is determined by the scroll-container clip, but whose backing store can over-allocate on some GPU tile budgets. The sibling `overflow: clip` on `.marquee-track` helps but does not bound the promoted layer's internal size.
findings.proposed: Add `contain: layout style` to `.marquee-inner` alongside the existing `will-change: transform`. This bounds the layout recalculation to the marquee subtree and lets the compositor allocate the tile region based on the clipped viewport rather than the full `max-content` width. Alternatively, set `will-change: auto` and let the browser decide (the CSS animation already qualifies the element for a composited layer without the explicit hint). Given the PRM guard already stops the animation under reduce, `will-change: auto` is cleaner.

findings.title: ConvergencePlot per-frame resize: canvas dimensions set inside the draw call every rAF tick
findings.evidence: web/src/components/equation/ConvergencePlot.vue:82–89. `draw()` calls `canvas.getBoundingClientRect()` and sets `canvas.width`/`canvas.height` on every call, including inside the 60fps rAF loop. Setting canvas dimensions triggers a layout read (getBoundingClientRect) and then a canvas pixel-buffer reallocation every frame — even when the container size has not changed.
findings.current_state: Every tick of the rAF loop performs a layout-triggering DOM read and a canvas pixel-buffer re-create (clearing the canvas is implied). On a stable layout this means 60 unnecessary canvas resets per second. On a resize this is correct behaviour, but it should be gated by a ResizeObserver. The M plan names this explicitly: 'fix the ConvergencePlot per-frame resize' in M.W9's consumer bullet.
findings.proposed: M.W9: mirror the `useCanvasSetup` pattern from BasisCanvas.vue: use the existing `resizeObserver` (ConvergencePlot already creates one at line 325) to write cached `w`/`h`/`dpr` refs; the `draw()` function reads the cache and only resets `canvas.width`/`canvas.height` when the ResizeObserver fires. Remove `getBoundingClientRect()` from the hot draw path.

findings.title: View-Transitions router guard: double rAF release in afterEach is INP-unsafe on slow navigations
findings.evidence: web/src/router/index.ts (afterEach block, approx line 169–173): `requestAnimationFrame(() => requestAnimationFrame(release))`. The double-rAF ensures two paint frames before resolving the VT update callback. On a slow JS parse (e.g. after an aggressive back-forward cache eviction), two rAF ticks can span >100ms, holding the view-transition snapshot open and blocking input response.
findings.current_state: The double-rAF is the idiomatic pattern for 'wait for Vue to commit the new component tree' but it is conservative. If Vue's DOM patch completes before the first rAF (which it usually does via nextTick), the second rAF is purely an insurance delay that can extend the VT snapshot window beyond the comfortable INP budget (50ms target).
findings.proposed: Replace with `nextTick(() => requestAnimationFrame(release))`: Vue's nextTick fires after the DOM patch, the single rAF then waits for the paint frame. This is the minimal safe release sequence. If the VT looks jarring in practice (snapshot closes too early), the double-rAF can be restored as a documented exception per inv-34.

findings.title: play-btn rainbow-drift: background-position animation on a multi-stop gradient — compositor-unsafe
findings.evidence: web/src/components/visualization/AnimationControls.vue:163, 176, 187. `.play-btn::before` is a 7-stop rainbow gradient with `background-size: 300% 300%`. `.play-btn.is-playing::before` animates `background-position` — a non-compositable property that forces a repaint every frame while the animation plays.
findings.current_state: `background-position` animation (and by extension `background-size`) runs on the main thread paint tier, not the compositor. During epicycle playback the main thread is already busy with the rAF clock + canvas draw. The rainbow-drift animation adds a full repaint of the button's pseudo-element every frame, compounding the main-thread load. The M plan notes: 'move play-btn rainbow-drift to a compositor filter' in M.W9.
findings.proposed: M.W9: transpose to a `hue-rotate` CSS animation on the play button's `filter` property — `@keyframes hue-spin { to { filter: hue-rotate(360deg); } }`. `filter` is compositor-eligible on Chromium/Safari/Firefox. The multi-stop gradient becomes a single-stop vivid base colour; `hue-rotate` cycles it. This is a compositor-path animation at zero additional paint cost. PRM guard already present (AnimationControls.vue:178–179).

findings.title: Multiple bare `ease`/`ease-in`/`ease-out` keyword usages not using design tokens (A.W3.d residue)

E6.dimension: Motion-architecture transposition (E6) — the unified M motion CORE: CSS-first → glass-ui motion composables → keyframes 4.3 light primitives + value.js 0.13 colour motion; retire the manual rAF loop; the convergence-reveal signature.
E6.verdict: M-motion-architecture.md is the strongest of the M design docs — its three-layer rule, its rAF inventory, its `useFourierPlayhead` contract, and its convergence-reveal signature are architecturally sound and survive my source re-verification at HEAD. It needs HARDENING, not re-derivation, on six load-bearing points the bump moved underneath it: (1) keyframes is now 4.3.0 (the doc/charter say 4.2) and ships a NEW `ScrollScene`/`createScrollScene` "Scroll-as-CSS" primitive that supersedes part of §5; (2) keyframes 4.3 ships ONE flat barrel — the doc's central "light static-barrel vs heavy `loadAnimationEngine()` import path" distinction is now FALSE (it is a tree-shaking concern, not an import-path one), and §0/§1 must say so or a reader will author a non-existent import; (3) the router View-Transition site (#10) is MISCHARACTERIZED — at HEAD it is already a clean `beforeResolve`/`afterEach` promise-bracket over glass-ui's `supportsViewTransitions()`+`prefersReducedMotion()`, so the transposition is far smaller than "retire a hand-rolled wrap"; (4) `SvgFilters.vue:51` is an rAF site the inventory omits (one-shot warm-up, EXEMPT-class — but it must be NAMED so the close-gate's "zero rAF" sweep does not trip on it); (5) ConvergencePlot already DECLARES a `ResizeObserver` (`:48`) it never wires — the per-frame-resize fix is connecting dead substrate, not adding new; (6) value.js 0.13 ships `sampleColorRamp` + `PathGeometry`/`getPointAtLength`, which lets the convergence-reveal's colour-motion AND its arc-length draw-on run at LIGHT tier, killing the doc's open worry that draw-on forces the heavy `DrawSVG` engine. Net: the architecture is right; the API surface it cites drifted one minor + one major and must be re-pinned. The signature (convergence-reveal) and the layering rule are KEEP-AS-IS. The motion CORE traces to two of the eight live critiques (idle-button-paint #6 and tabs-as-glass #7 carry a state-transition motion facet) and stays inv-34-governed.

findings.title: useCanvasHover's TWO rAF loops (#5 scale-smoother + #6 shimmer) must collapse to ZERO private loops, not two replacements — the shimmer is a phase read off the scene clock
findings.evidence: visualization/composables/useCanvasHover.ts:52-63 (`updateHoverScale`: `currentScale += diff*0.12` magic factor, own rAF at :62); :67-82 (`startShimmer`/`shimmerTick`: a perpetual `onRedraw()` loop while a label is hovered, own rAF at :72,74); M-motion-architecture.md:91-92 (#5→SpringProgress, #6→'fold into the single scene playhead')
findings.current_state: The hover composable owns TWO independent rAF loops: a hand-rolled exponential scale smoother (the magic `0.12` factor) and a perpetual shimmer redraw that runs even when the scene is PAUSED (it re-samples the wall-clock golden-shimmer every frame while a label is hovered). The doc correctly maps #5→`SpringProgress` and #6→fold-into-scene-clock, but the two are entangled (both call `onRedraw`) and the shimmer's pause-time behaviour is the subtle one: when `playing===false` but a label is hovered, today a SECOND rAF spins. This is exactly the §6.2 'no second rAF' rule and the most error-prone part of the collapse (the doc's §17.7 risk note flags the off-screen-park regression risk).
findings.proposed: Collapse to: (a) the scale smoother → `SpringProgress({response,dampingFraction,respectReducedMotion:true})` driven by the SCENE playhead's frame hook (not its own loop) — `spring.target = inRegion ? hoverScale : baseScale`, read `spring.value` in the scene's `onFrame`, the `0.12` magic factor DELETED; (b) the shimmer → a PURE phase read off the shared playhead's `now` (the §4/§6.1 'shimmer is a phase, not a loop' rule), so when the scene is paused there is NO redraw and the shimmer freezes (correct — a paused scene shows a static frame). The single hard case — paused-scene + hovered-label wanting a live spring settle — is handled by the playhead exposing a 'drive-until-settle' one-shot (`RAFPlayback.drive(spring, redraw)` auto-stops on settle, §2 #5 idiom) rather than reviving a perpetual loop. Result: `useCanvasHover` owns ZERO autonomous rAF; the two loops become a spring + a clock-phase read. Add this as an explicit M.W9 sub-step with the paused+hovered case named, because the doc currently under-specifies the entanglement.

findings.title: useFourierPlayhead must expose a clock-phase accessor for the wall-clock oscillators (golden-shimmer + epicycles) — §6.1's 'drive now from the shared playhead' has no surface in the §3 contract
findings.evidence: M-motion-architecture.md:94 (#8: oscillators `0.85+0.15*sin(now/200)` and `0.2+0.1*sin(now/300)` → 'Drive now from the shared playhead clock'); :226 (§6.1 gap 1 same); §3 `FourierPlayhead` interface (:126-137) exposes `t`/`easedT`/`playing`/`isPaused` but NO raw `now`/`elapsedMs` clock phase
findings.current_state: §6.1 and inventory #8 both require the two wall-clock shimmer oscillators to 'drive `now` from the shared playhead clock' (so PRM gates them and a paused scene stops the pulse). But the §3 `useFourierPlayhead` interface exposes only the normalized phase `t`/`easedT` — there is no accessor for an absolute/elapsed clock phase the `sin(now/200)` oscillators need. The oscillators read wall-clock `performance.now()` at a DIFFERENT cadence than the 0→1 ping-pong phase; you cannot reconstruct `sin(now/200)` from `t∈[0,1]` alone without the cycle count + duration.
findings.proposed: Add a `clockMs: Readonly<Ref<number>>` (the playhead's accumulated, PRM-zeroed, pause-frozen elapsed milliseconds) to the §3 `FourierPlayhead` interface — the single monotonic phase the shimmer oscillators read (`0.85+0.15*sin(clockMs/200)`), which (a) freezes when paused (no pulse), (b) zeroes its oscillation amplitude under PRM via the playhead's own gate (the terminal-mean, §6.1), and (c) is the SAME clock the convergence-reveal `Sequence` seeks. This closes the §3↔§6.1 contract gap: the oscillators become pure functions of `clockMs`, owning no rAF and inheriting PRM + pause for free. Without it, #8's fix has nothing to bind to.

findings.title: The idle-button-paint (critique #6) and tabs-as-glass (critique #7) carry a STATE-TRANSITION motion facet the motion CORE must claim under Layer 1 — not leave to ad-hoc per-component CSS
findings.evidence: user-critique/09 (preset pills bare text, no idle paint — only hover/active shows a chip); user-critique/10 (tabs underline, want glass); CRITIQUE.md:12-13 (#6 tonal-accent idle fill, #7 glass tab variant); M-motion-architecture.md:72 (Layer-1 rule covers 'hover/transition micro-motion') but §2/§4/§5 never name the control-state idle↔hover↔active transition as a CORE concern

The visible defect is a design/adoption gap (E2/E4's charge), but the TRANSITION between those states — the active-pill slide on `SegmentedTabs`, the tonal-fill cross-fade on the pills — is motion, and it belongs to Layer 1 (`transition`/`@keyframes`, PRM-gated in CSS, off-main-thread). State the boundary: the design waves OWN the resting paint; the motion CORE OWNS the transition contract (so PRM is inherited, not re-carved per component). This is the motion-side trace of critiques #6/#7 and prevents 25 components each hand-rolling a non-PRM transition.

findings.title: The convergence-reveal once-latch and the §3 playhead share a remount hazard with the paper virtual-window — the signature must key first-paint by a STABLE viz id, not a mount event
findings.evidence: M-motion-architecture.md:164 (signature trigger 'every canvas/spectrum first-paint'); :194,200-202 (§5.2 the virtual/teleporting section window re-fires reveals on remount → the once-discipline `Set<string>` keyed by section id); BasisCanvas data-watcher cited :378-394; §3 contract 4 (the store becomes a STATE atom, canvases register/deregister as they mount)
findings.current_state: §5.2 correctly identifies the virtual-window remount hazard for SCROLL reveals and fixes it with a `Set<string>` once-latch. But the §4 convergence-reveal has the SAME hazard and the doc does not connect them: a `BasisCanvas` or `ConvergencePlot` that unmounts (off-screen / route swap / fullscreen toggle — two canvases mount per the §3 ref-count) and remounts would re-fire the 'first-paint' settle every time, replaying the 900ms reveal on a figure the user already saw. 'First-paint' defined as a mount event is wrong for a virtualized/dual-mount surface.
findings.proposed: Define the convergence-reveal trigger as 'first DATA-ARRIVAL for a given visualization IDENTITY', keyed by `visualizationSlug` (the same key the §3 store uses to reach the canvas) in a module-level `Set<string>` — a remounted or second-instance canvas of an already-revealed viz paints its TERMINAL state immediately (no replay), exactly mirroring §5.2's section once-latch. State this in §4.1 and cross-reference §5.2 so the two once-latches are ONE discipline (and the booked glass-ui `convergence-reveal` preset, §4.3, carries the `{ once, key }` contract the same way `useStaggerReveal({once,key})` does). Without this, the signature flickers on every off-screen return — the precise defect §5.2 was written to prevent, un-applied to §4.

findings.title: Easing-unification is named but the catalog is not inventoried — `lib/easings.ts` (the store's ANIMATION_EASINGS) vs value.js easeInOut* vs keyframes resolveEasing must be reconciled to one source
findings.evidence: stores/animation.ts:3-7 (imports `ANIMATION_EASINGS`/`getEasingSVGPath` from `@/lib/easings`); :27-30 (easedT applies a fourier-local easing fn); useCurveTransition.ts:8 (imports `easeInOutSine` from value.js directly); ConvergencePlot.vue:34 (also `easeInOutSine` from value.js); M.md:85 ('unify the easing catalog on keyframes resolveEasing + spring twins'); M-motion-architecture.md:32,264 names the boundary but no inventory
findings.current_state: There are THREE easing sources in play: (1) fourier-local `lib/easings.ts` `ANIMATION_EASINGS` (the user-selectable easing catalog the animation store + the easing-picker UI consume, with SVG-path previews); (2) value.js `easeInOut*` imported DIRECTLY at two sites (`useCurveTransition`, `ConvergencePlot`); (3) keyframes' `resolveEasing`/`toEasing` boundary the doc names as the normalizer. The charter says 'unify on keyframes resolveEasing + spring twins' but neither doc inventories `lib/easings.ts` — which is the USER-FACING catalog (the picker), a distinct concern from the internal lerp easing. Collapsing them blindly risks losing the SVG-path preview surface the picker needs.
findings.proposed: Inventory the three sources in §2 (or a new §6.5) and draw the boundary explicitly: (a) `lib/easings.ts` STAYS as the user-facing CATALOG (it owns the named set + the SVG-path previews for the picker UI — a presentation concern keyframes doesn't serve), but its `fn` values are re-sourced from value.js curves through keyframes' `toEasing` so there is ONE curve authority (value.js) and ONE boundary (keyframes `resolveEasing`); (b) the two direct `easeInOutSine`-from-value.js imports route through the playhead/SmoothProgress easing param (not called inline in `draw()`), so the curve is applied once-per-frame at the clock, not re-evaluated per-point. State that the catalog is NOT deleted (it serves the picker) — only the DUPLICATE inline curve evaluation is. This prevents the 'unify easing' line from being read as 'delete lib/easings.ts' (which would break the picker — a legacy-introducing over-reach).

glassui_asks.name: convergence-reveal motion preset
glassui_asks.what: A canonical 'partial-sum settle' motion preset: a spring + orchestration descriptor (series-settle + harmonic-accumulation stagger + arc-length draw-on) carrying a PRM-collapse-to-terminal contract and a `{ once, key }` first-paint latch, where the consumer drives a normalized accumulation phase into its own per-element progress curve (for fourier, `harmonicProgress(idx,total,revealT)`).
glassui_asks.why: It is fourier's signature motion (the series visibly converging onto its target) and the grammar generalizes to ANY progressive-accumulation reveal (value.js palette-ramp build, a metric-stack count-up cascade, a deck-bar rise) — so the spring constants + the orchestration timing + the PRM + once-latch contract belong in the shared motion layer, not hand-rolled per consumer. fourier composes the interim locally from the already-shipped light primitives (SpringProgress+Sequence+stagger) + value.js sampleColorRamp/PathGeometry and consumes-and-deletes when the preset ships at the glass-ui 4.1.0 cut.

glassui_asks.name: useCharStagger / SplitChars (a11y-name-preserving glyph splitter)
glassui_asks.what: A composable/utility that splits a heading's text into per-glyph spans, sets `--char-index`, and PRESERVES the accessible name (`aria-label` on the parent, `aria-hidden` on the shards) + text selection — so the shipped `.char-stagger` CSS recipe (typography.css) can drive a per-glyph entrance cascade without breaking screen-reader output or copy/paste.
glassui_asks.why: glass-ui 4.0 ships the `.char-stagger` CSS recipe but NOT the glyph-split that feeds it; every consumer hand-rolling the split will re-introduce the a11y-name hazard. fourier wants it for the paper hero masthead entrance (PRM-gated, once-disciplined, ≤600ms). Until it ships fourier hand-rolls the split scoped to the single hero title.

glassui_asks.name: [data-scroll-reveal="once"] cross-remount latch (or useStaggerReveal({once,key}))
glassui_asks.what: A variant of the shipped `[data-scroll-reveal]` (scroll-driven.css) `view()` recipe that keys reveal-state by a stable id in an external Set, so a section that unmounts and remounts (a virtualized/teleporting window) reads as already-revealed and renders at end-state with NO re-animation.
glassui_asks.why: glass-ui's `useStaggerReveal` composable honours `once` but the NATIVE CSS recipe has no cross-remount latch — and fourier's paper has a virtual/teleporting section window (`useVirtualSectionWindow` + `useScrollNavigation` teleport) that re-fires the recipe on every re-entry → flicker. The same once-latch discipline also governs fourier's convergence-reveal (so the two are one contract). Interim: fourier scopes a header-only fourier-local Set keyed by section id.

glassui_asks.name: canvas-anchored specular overlay (synthetic-rect variant of useSpecularTracking)
glassui_asks.what: A variant of the shipped `useSpecularTracking` that accepts a SYNTHETIC bounding rect (a sub-region of a `<canvas>`) rather than measuring a DOM element each frame — so a glass BAND-1 panel floating over a bright canvas region gets the pointer-anchored catch-light without a per-frame getBoundingClientRect on the hot path.
glassui_asks.why: `useSpecularTracking` shipped at 4.0 (confirmed — it does ONE rect-measure per rAF-coalesced frame, the correct INP pattern), which STRIKES the older `useSpecular` ask. The still-open net-new is the canvas-region case: fourier's distinctive surface is `<canvas>`, and a panel's catch-light should track the pointer relative to a canvas sub-region (a synthetic rect), preserving the one-measure-per-frame INP discipline rather than re-measuring.
